steps.say: Darling's anatomical classification categorises anomalous venous drainage into four distinct patterns based on the site of systemic connection.
steps.tx: Anatomical mapping follows the **Darling classification**. Darling classification divides TAPVC into Type I Supracardiac (**45%**), Type II Cardiac (**25%**), Type III Infracardiac (**20-25%**), and Type IV Mixed (**5%**), based upon the specific site of systemic venous termination. Comprehensive evaluation and serial clinical assessments remain essential to guide individualized management and ensure optimal patient outcomes.

steps.say: Unobstructed supracardiac drainage produces a celebrated radiographic contour on chest radiography in older surviving infants.
steps.tx: Chest radiography demonstrates the **snowman sign**. The classic snowman sign (figure-of-8 appearance) on CXR is characteristic of unobstructed Type I supracardiac TAPVC, formed by the dilated left vertical vein, innominate vein, and right superior vena cava atop an enlarged right heart. Comprehensive evaluation and serial clinical assessments remain essential to guide individualized management and ensure optimal patient outcomes.

steps.say: Subdiaphragmatic drainage carries an exceptionally high frequency of severe anatomical obstruction that precipitates rapid neonatal pulmonary edema.
steps.tx: Subdiaphragmatic variants feature severe **infracardiac obstruction**. Type III infracardiac TAPVC drains below the diaphragm into the portal vein or ductus venosus and is almost universally obstructed (>95%), presenting with severe pulmonary venous hypertension, profound hypoxemia, and acute respiratory distress within hours of birth.

left.title: Anatomical Pathway of Obstruction
points: Long descending vertical vein courses through esophageal hiatus of diaphragm
Drains into portal vein, ductus venosus, or hepatic vascular sinusoids
Extrinsic compression by diaphragm and intrinsic high hepatic resistance

right.title: Clinical Emergency Presentation
points: Severe obstruction to pulmonary venous return develops in >95% of infants
Fulminant neonatal pulmonary edema, severe lactic acidosis, and cyanosis
Mandates immediate emergency surgical repair within hours of birth

steps.say: Because all venous return enters the right side of the heart, systemic perfusion is entirely dependent upon an open interatrial communication.
steps.tx: Systemic perfusion mandates an **obligatory right-to-left ASD**. An unrestrictive atrial septal defect is mandatory to allow oxygenated blood to enter the left atrium and systemic circulation; restrictive ASD causes profound low cardiac output and systemic hypoperfusion. Comprehensive evaluation and serial clinical assessments remain essential to guide individualized management and ensure optimal patient outcomes.

nodes.label: All four pulmonary veins drain abnormally into systemic venous channels
Complete systemic and pulmonary venous mixing occurs in the right atrium
Obligatory right-to-left shunting across patent foramen ovale or ASD
Supplies essential systemic output to left ventricle and arterial tree

steps.say: Complete mixing of pulmonary and systemic venous return produces uniform oxygen saturations across all four cardiac chambers.
steps.tx: Intracardiac oximetry documents **identical saturations**. Complete mixing in the right atrium results in identical oxygen saturation in all four cardiac chambers and the great arteries, typically ranging between **75-85%** in unobstructed forms with high pulmonary blood flow. Comprehensive evaluation and serial clinical assessments remain essential to guide individualized management and ensure optimal patient outcomes.

left.title: Oximetric Triad in TAPVC
points: Complete mixing of systemic and pulmonary venous return in right atrium
Identical saturations in RA, RV, PA, LA, LV, and systemic aorta
Resting arterial saturation typically 75% to 85% in unobstructed defects

right.title: Differentiating Features
points: D-TGA: Reversed saturation differential (PA saturation higher than aorta)
Truncus Arteriosus: Near-equal saturations in aorta and pulmonary trunk
Normal Circulation: Distinct systemic (75%) vs pulmonary venous (98%) saturations

steps.say: Acute pulmonary venous obstruction precipitates severe pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock requiring emergent operative intervention.
steps.tx: Obstructed neonates require **emergency surgery for obstructed TAPVC**. Obstructed TAPVC is a true surgical emergency; balloon septostomy is ineffective for pulmonary venous obstruction, and emergent surgical anastomosis of the pulmonary venous confluence to the left atrium is life-saving. Comprehensive evaluation and serial clinical assessments remain essential to guide individualized management and ensure optimal patient outcomes.

steps.say: Direct drainage into the coronary sinus or right atrium constitutes the intracardiac subtype with favorable surgical exposure.
steps.tx: Intracardiac connections represent **cardiac type drainage**. Type II cardiac TAPVC drains directly into the coronary sinus or right atrium, where surgical repair involves unroofing the coronary sinus into the left atrium and closing the atrial septal defect with a pericardial patch. Comprehensive evaluation and serial clinical assessments remain essential to guide individualized management and ensure optimal patient outcomes.

left.title: Coronary Sinus Drainage
points: Pulmonary veins enter coronary sinus, causing massive coronary sinus dilation
Surgically unroofed into the left atrium with patch closure of the ASD
Excellent long-term outcomes with minimal risk of pulmonary vein obstruction

right.title: Right Atrial Drainage
points: Pulmonary veins enter directly into posterior wall of right atrium
Baffled across the atrial septum into left atrium using pericardial patch
Requires careful avoidance of sinus node and AV node conduction injury

steps.say: Postoperative narrowing of the individual or confluent pulmonary veins poses a grave late management challenge.
steps.tx: Late surveillance watches for **postoperative pulmonary vein stenosis**. Recurrent pulmonary vein stenosis occurs in **10-15%** of postoperative patients, carries a poor prognosis, and may require sutureless repair techniques or catheter-directed stenting to preserve lung vascular beds. Comprehensive evaluation and serial clinical assessments remain essential to guide individualized management and ensure optimal patient outcomes.
